newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Russian minister meets Arafat, optimistic on peace.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister meets Arafat, optimistic on peace.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said after meeting Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in self-ruled Gaza on Friday he was confident that Middle East peace talks would produce results.

"The process may take a few months so things could move forward. But everybody should know that there is light at the end of the tunnel," Primakov, speaking through an interpreter, told reporters at a news conference with Arafat.
He said Russia would activate its role in Middle East peace efforts. He did not elaborate. Russia is a co-sponsor with the United States of Middle East peace talks that began in 1991.
Primakov said peace efforts would suffer if any party reneged on the principle of trading occupied land for peace enshrined in the Madrid conference that launched the talks.
Primakov is on a Middle East tour that has taken him to Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and Israel. He arrived in Gaza from Israel on Friday after assuring Israel that Syria did not seek war.

Israeli negotiations with Syria and Lebanon, suspended before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ousted Labour party's Shimon Peres in Israel's elections in May, have yet to resume. Netanyahu opposes trading occupied Arab land for peace.
Israel-PLO talks on implementing an Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron are snagged on security issues.
Arafat said Primakov's first visit to the Palestinian self-rule areas was important to push forward the talks on Hebron. He said the talks were "foundering".
Israel on Friday removed a general who had met Peres behind the government's back from its peace negotiating team with the PLO.

A Defence Ministry statement said Major-General Oren Shahor was suspended from the negotiating team pending an investigation but would remain Israel's so-called chief coordinator of government activities in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Shahor drew political fire after an Israeli newspaper published a front-page photo on Thursday showing him leaving the home of former Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres and reported he had also met former cabinet minister Yossi Beilin.
Primakov met Netanyahu in West Jerusalem on Thursday and tried to calm war jitters in the Jewish state.
"While in Damascus, and I told the prime minister, I had no impression that the Syrians were preparing any strike against Israel," Primakov said.
Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi on Friday urged the Syrian army to attack and take back the Golan Heights it lost to Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

"The Syrian army must enter the Golan and liberate it by force," Gaddafi told a news conference in Tunis. He also urged Lebanon's army to join pro-Iranian guerrillas fighting to drive Israeli troops from an occupied border strip in south Lebanon.
Arafat returned to Gaza on Friday from a European tour to seek support for persuading Israel to implement self-rule deals.
"I explained to (the Europeans) the situation concerning the peace process and the obstacles...which are preventing the implementation of the signed agreement," he said on arrival.

Israel had criticised Arafat's trip as an effort to delay a Hebron agreement, speculating he wanted to wait until after U.S. elections on November 5, hoping a new administration would pressure Israel. Arafat has denied the charges.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk held an unscheduled meeting with Netanyahu after the cabinet's weekly session, which discussed Hebron. Israel Radio said Netanyahu asked for the meeting but gave no details of what was discussed.

The main U.S. mediator in four weeks of Israel-PLO talks on Hebron, Dennis Ross, returned home this week after the sides failed to strike a deal over terms for the redeployment from the town where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs.
Israeli and Palestinian negotiators continued talks while Ross and Arafat were away. U.S. officials said they did not expect Ross to return before the middle of next week.
